content.content:
later.py: his messages after an entry's creation that may bear on it, though no commit of the
entry followed them (his later word may have gone into a skill or another record instead).

    python3 -I later.py 148                   (or P-148)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --top 25          how many to print (default 15)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --at 36f7db77c --until 2026-10-21T20:54
                                              the entry's text at a commit, and no message after a time

The candidates are his messages in the coordinating sessions (tlib.COORDINATING) from the entry's
creation on (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md, its last text is read, and the list runs on
past the removal) (the first commit of its trail that made its text), less those that leads.py already
printed near the entry's own commits. Each is scored by the entry's distinctive terms:
  - its title's words, beyond common words (a stop list, and words in more than a tenth of his
    messages), lightly stemmed (possessive and plural off, cut to 7 letters); each weighs its
    rarity in his messages, log(messages / messages holding it);
  - its names in backticks, weight 3 each.
A term in his own words (lines that do not start with ">") counts whole; a term only in the
exchange around his message (the coordinator's message he answered, by the reply chain, its
reply to him, and the lines he quoted) counts half. A message also gains 8 when it falls in the
30 minutes before a commit that changed a file the entry names in backticks (`compiler.md`), other
than the entry's own commits, in lines that hold a title term (3 when the lines hold none): that
is where his word may have gone. Naming the entry's number (P-148, or as dictated, P148) adds 8 in
his words, 2 in the exchange. A message is a candidate when its weight is at least 5 (MIN) and it
holds a term in his own words or falls before such a commit. Printed: rank, weight, time, whether it
is after the entry's last change, the terms (in parentheses when only in the exchange), the commit
it precedes, and its first 300 characters; then how many candidates there were in all.

homes.py: where a status that an entry of POSITIONS.md states may already live.

    python3 -I homes.py 151            (or P-151)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --top 8    candidates per sentence (default 5)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --at REV   the three files as commit REV holds them

Splits the entry (the working tree's POSITIONS.md; for an entry struck from it, its text as it
last stood, said so at the top) into sentences, and a sentence into its clauses
at the semicolons outside parentheses; a clause keeps the label that opens its sentence, as
"Built:" or "Still to build:". A clause states a status when it, its label or its sentence holds
one of the status words: built, to build, landed, pending, default, waits, standing go, listed for his
review, open, held, parked, owed, taken, stands at, returns after, not moved, and the like.

For each such clause it lists the candidates that may already hold the same point: the numbered
items of review-queue.md's lists (b) and (c), and the lines of PLAN.md (a numbered sub-line also
carries its parent's item number, and its own number as a fork when the parent counts forks).
A candidate is listed when it names the entry or shares a distinctive term with the clause:
  row N, item N (PLAN's), review-queue item N, fork N, way N, batch N, rung X, phase N, ask N,
  decision X, another entry's P-N, a name in backticks (a commit hash too), a dotted finding
  name such as judge-review.1 or A.skeptic.2
pointers.py: every line of the record that names an entry of POSITIONS.md by its number.

    python3 -I pointers.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I pointers.py 86 --at REV   the files as commit REV holds them

Searches, at the working tree: explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, POSITIONS.md, PLAN.md,
review-queue.md, HELD.md and BOOT.md; explorations/reviews/open-asks-*.md; and every file under
.claude/skills/. The history files (POSITIONS-history.md, FACTS-history.md) are not searched:
trail.py reads the first, and both only record. A line counts when it holds the number as a word:
P-86 matches, as in "P-86's" or "(P-86)", but P-860 and P-186 do not. A line that names a range
holding the number ("P-85 to P-88") is listed too, marked as a range.
Prints path:line and the line (cut at 400 characters around the number; --whole prints it whole),
grouped by file; the entry's own line in POSITIONS.md is marked.

comments.py: his saved page comments that bear on an entry of POSITIONS.md.

    python3 -I comments.py 66            (or P-66)

He also comments on pages, and those comments are not in the transcripts. They are saved as
explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/evidence/curator-comments-*.md: a section per thread,
headed "## On <what it was anchored to>", with one bullet per comment, "- HH:MM: "words"".
A section counts when its heading, or a comment counts when its own words, either
  - name the entry's number, also as dictated: P-66, P66, PE66, P 66 (not P-660), or
  - quote its title: a quoted run ("..." or curly quotes) of at least three content words, at
    least 60 % of which are words of the entry's bold title (case, possessives and punctuation
    ignored).
A section that counts is printed whole, with its heading; a comment that counts in another
section is printed with that section's heading. Each with its file and line.

  NO MATCH     neither; it then prints the longest run of the quote's words that the

hischeck.py: check the block of his quotes that a scout's or reader's report ends with.

    python3 -I hischeck.py FILE...

Each FILE holds a block headed "## His quotes" (to the next "## " heading or the end), one line
per quote of his:
    HIS 2026-09-26T10:21:32.097Z | Run Fable judgement as well.
(a line may be wrapped in backticks or start with "- "). The time is a prefix of his message's
timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z dropped); each message of his at that time is tried,
and the quote is checked as quote.py does:
  EXACT        a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once whitespace is collapsed and U+2019 made a straight apostrophe
  NO MATCH     neither, in every message at that time (quote.py "QUOTE" TIME shows the nearest run)
  NO MESSAGE   no message of his at that time
Lines of the block that start with HIS but do not parse are counted as BAD FORM. Prints, per
file, the counts and every line that is not EXACT or NORMALISED, with its line number; exits 1
when any line fails or a file has no block.

Prints:

     commit that removed it and the reason its history block gives, and the text as it last stood);
  2. its blocks in POSITIONS-history.md at HEAD, each with the commit that wrote it (the oldest
     commit whose history file holds the block's provenance line). A block's own "commit X" names
     the source it cites, not its writer;
  3. every commit that made or changed the entry's text, oldest first, read from each commit's own

     the text before was made (number, line, title: exact; similarity: score printed), how many
     other entries of POSITIONS.md the commit changed, and the reasons on record: the history
     blocks it wrote, the comments above verbatim copies of the text in the old history file, and
     the commit message.
  4. a cross-check: the old history lines that the numbering block names as earlier texts of this
     entry, and whether each is a text of this trail.

**What should an integer raised to a negative power give, such as `2^(-1)`?**

**Context**
- **This replaces Haiku's ask on this item from today,** whose figures were stale and two of its claims wrong.
- **Where the integer power stands today.** Every integer `^` in the interpreter's library is declared `RR64`, a float. Walk gives `2^3` = `8` and `2^(-1)` = `0.5`. The compiled path gives `2^(-1)` = `0`, because its native converts the result of Java's `Math.pow` to an `int`.
- **The premise you've already taken:** each integer `^` answers its own type, so `2^3` is `8 : ZZ32`.
  - That keeps integer code exact, such as the library's `strToInt`, which sums `d radix^(n-i)`.
  - The exponent stays signed, since it's often computed, as `n-i` is there.
  - So `2^(-1)` needs a `ZZ32` value, or none. That's the fork.
- **The team's earlier text.** The Working Draft of 2011 gave `2^(-1)` = 1/2: ℤ was then inside ℚ, and a signed exponent went to the rationals' power.
- **The team's later word.** The compiled library gives every exponent an integer type. The later word wins, and that's your premise.
  - On the value it says nothing you can weigh. Its 0 is a side effect of the conversion.
  - Guy Steele's helper that answers 0 is unfinished, nothing calls it, and it also gives 0 for `0^(-1)`.
  - The revival's chapter leaves the value open.
- **The library's own way.** A result that a fixed-width integer type can't hold raises `IntegerOverflow`. A fraction comes from a float or rational base: `10.0^(-4)`, or `(2/3)^(-1)` = `3/2`. microGPT writes `10.0^(-5)`.
- **How to judge.** The team's later word comes first, then its library, then the peer languages where the team conflicts or is silent. On the value the team is silent, so the peers weigh.
- **The peers.** Julia, Java's `BigInteger.pow` and Haskell's `^` raise an error. Rust types the exponent unsigned. X10 answers a float, as walk does today. Swift has no integer power. None answers 0.
- **The switch-over needs this answer,** before it and no sooner. Six of today's 34 distance sites are the power's.
  - The distance counts every error the compiled checker finds in the interpreter's library, and it must reach 0 before the switch-over.
  - The checker count is 30 today, all in the component that holds the six sites. The probe didn't measure it. It may fall with the six sites, or rise as the check reaches further.
- **microGPT.** No line changes under any option, since its own powers have a float base. Its one integer power is `strToInt`'s, when it reads its data. Its speed isn't at stake.

**Options**
1. **E, an error.**
   - `2^(-1)` raises `IntegerOverflow` and `0^(-1)` raises `DivisionByZero`. `1^(-1)` = 1 and `(-1)^(-1)` = −1.
   - It clears 5 sites, and the sixth with `fail[\ZZ32\]` written in `strToInt`, a one-line fix of its own: 34 to about 29, or 28.
   - 15 library edits (29 lines in, 27 out), plus 11 lines of walk natives.
   - microGPT's quick check passes, with every value equal.
   - Three team tests, `realArith`, `compoundArray` and `simpleExp`, raise at their negative powers and get a float base, such as `10.0^(-16)`. The demos `BiCGSTAB` and `BiCGSTAB2` would raise at `10^(-4)`.
2. **Z, zero.**
   - `2^(-1)` = 0, truncated toward zero. `0^(-1)` and the bases ±1 behave as in option 1.
   - The same library text, sites and microGPT result as option 1.
   - `realArith` fails its assert and `simpleExp` stops. `compoundArray` passes with six printed lines changed, such as 0.7071… to 0.0. The demos' stopping threshold `10^(-4)` becomes 0.0. The three tests need a float base too.
3. **R, a rational.**
   - A signed exponent gives a `QQ`: `2^(-1)` = 1/2. An unsigned or numeral exponent gives the integer.
   - It clears 4 sites and adds 2, leaving about 32. 21 edits (91 lines in, 29 out).
   - It needs Q-walk first, walk's half of the switch to the library's numeral type, planned with the switch-over's batches. Until then `2^3` is a `QQ` under walk, and 16 of the 26 walk tests that reach a power fail.
   - microGPT's quick check stops in `strToInt`.
4. **X, an unsigned exponent.**
   - `^` takes only an `NN32`, `NN64` or numeral exponent, so the checker refuses a signed one, such as `n-i`.
   - It clears 5 sites, leaving about 29. 23 edits (57 lines in, 31 out), and every caller with a signed exponent converts it, as in `radix^(unsigned(n-i))`.
   - It needs Q-walk first. Until then 16 of the 26 walk tests fail.
   - microGPT passes. The compiled `ZZ32 ^ ZZ32` and three compiled tests are removed. The team tests and demos change as in option 1.

**How they weigh**
- Options 1 and 2 cost the same, clear the same sites, and land in phase 3.
- Option 1 stops with an error where the three team tests use a negative power. It matches Julia, Java, Haskell, and the revival's own refusal of a negative exponent in a size. It gives up `2^(-1)` as a value, which a float or rational base gives instead.
- Option 2 keeps the compiled path's 0, but only the compiler's prelude binds that conversion, and the switch-over deletes the prelude. It changes a team test's printed values with no error, and no peer answers 0.
- Option 3 is the team's earlier design, which needed ℤ inside ℚ, and that went with the flat number tower. It clears the fewest sites, stops microGPT's check, and waits for Q-walk.
- Option 4 moves the error to the checker, as Rust does. It costs the most edits, a conversion in every caller with a signed exponent, and the wait for Q-walk.

I recommend option 1, with the three team tests given a float base and `fail[\ZZ32\]` written in the same rung. The full argument: https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/reviews/integer-power-negative-exponent.md

- P-80 **The sign-refined number types are a superseded design: a program tests such a subset at run time.** The number chapters test a value's sign by comparison, and a float's finiteness by `check` or `check*` on `RR64`. `advanced-lib/numbers-advanced.tex` stays word for word, marked superseded in the S1 form (P-96), so that the original design stays on record. Built. Their return with covariance is P-62's.
- P-153 **An integer raised to a negative power raises an error; a fraction comes from a float or rational base (contract E, item 58).** Each integer type's `^` answers its own type at every exponent: a negative exponent raises `IntegerOverflow` where the result is no integer, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code types an integer power by its integer at a signed exponent (P-26); overloads choose by type, and no type carries an exponent's or a numeral's sign, so the split is on the base, with the sign tested at run time as the library tests every sign-refined subset (P-80). Built in the one library and under walk. Still to build: the compiled path's own powers by the same contract, which answer 0 at a negative exponent today, when phase 4's natives bind the one library's `^` (rows 441 and 523; PLAN, phase 4, the natives).
59:- P-62 **The `covariant` keyword is future work, off the path to microGPT.** Row 404 records the hole: the checker accepts variance, and neither path carries it to run time. Its expected-failure tests are owed in a batch rung. The ledger's worklist item 12 is declaration-site variance, carried to run time on both paths. When it lands, the specification's sign-refined number types come back as covariant static parameters.
101:- P-96 **The S1 form: a change of the specification is shown in the layered form that the team used for 1.0 and its 2009 draft.** A callout that prints in every build, not a `\note`, marks each changed passage. Appendix I's revival section gives each change its reason, its original text, the way back to route C and the decision it follows. The front matter has one paragraph on the revision, and a repository document holds the full reasoning. The unrevised copy is cited as the Working Draft of February 2011. \chapter{Numbers}
\chaplabel{lib:numbers-advanced}
\revision{revival-superseded}{This chapter is the original design of the
rational types, kept word for word as a superseded design.
It defines the eighteen rational types of the Working Draft of February 2011
as instantiations of one trait, \TYP{RationalQuantity}, each of which extends
the instantiations with weaker flags.
Instantiation exclusion (\secref{revival-rule}) refuses that trait; the
compiled type checker refuses it as a cyclic type hierarchy, and the
interpreter cannot instantiate it; \library\ never declared these types; and
the team's later Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) comments out the type aliases

types are mutually exclusive (\secref{types-libraries}).

the library declares, and \appref{spec-changes} says why.
The way back is the later chapter's declaration-site variance: each flag a
covariant static parameter, a form the compiled type checker already accepts.
It waits for covariance to run on both implementations, which is item~12 of
the revival's worklist and row~404 of its gap ledger.}

7323 2026-09-26T11:39:32.529Z assistant TEXT: Recorded (`f206afcb7`). Batch 6's spec change keeps the advanced chapter word for word and marks it as a superseded design. It points to the road back: when variance runs (row 404, worklist item 12), try the sign flags as `covariant` parameters. The clean worker's probe of that shape (`Q3Phantom`) already passes the compiler's checker. It fails only at run time, which is exactly the variance gap.

**Can other languages express it?** This comes from my general knowledge, not checked in this session. The design has four parts: flags in the type, the type unchanged in memory, arithmetic that computes the result's flags, and "ℚ⁺ is usable where ℚ≥ is expected". How far peers get:
- **C++** can express all four, with templates over yes/no parameters and compile-time functions. Boost.Units does the units part this way. Subtyping becomes conversions the compiler permits only when the flags allow it.
- **Haskell** (type-level booleans and type families) and **Scala 3** (match types) can compute the result flags. There is no subtyping, so every widening is an explicit conversion. Scala's `refined` and `iron` libraries do a lighter version.
- **Rust** can hold the flags as `const bool` parameters. Computing result flags from them isn't stable yet. Its `uom` crate does the units part at the type level.
- **Proof assistants** (Lean, Coq, Agda) express it natively: a positive rational is "a rational with a proof it's positive". Lean even has a tactic, `positivity`, that automates exactly the sign reasoning the flags do.
- **Refinement-type systems** (Liquid Haskell, F*) come closest to the intent. You write `{v: Rational | v > 0}`, and a solver infers and checks the signs through arithmetic, with no 18 declared types.

**Where the research line is.** The Fortress version combines two things no mainstream language has together: native subtyping between instantiations, ordered by the flags, and multiple dispatch on those types. That combination is probably why the team never built it.
- **The resurrection as planned is engineering.** Covariant flag parameters, variance carried at run time (row 404), and result flags computed from six yes/no values are all decidable and fairly mechanical, and the checker already accepts the encoding.
- **What would be research** is getting the flags inferred through arithmetic without the programmer writing them. That's the refinement-type problem Liquid Haskell solves with an automated prover.

**Next, answer 8: what happens when a 32-bit and a 64-bit number meet?** Answer 7, the `SUM` replacement, waits for Astra's verdict. Answer 8 comes in my next message unless you want a pause.

### The designs

  `RationalQuantity[\U, ninf', ...\] where { bool ninf', ..., ninf -> ninf', ... }`, and
  conditionally `Field`, `AbelianGroup`, the order and lattice traits (:261-290);
  it coerces `Identity[\+\]`, `Identity[\DOT\]`, the `Zero`s and `IntegerQuantity`
  (:291-298); its operators compute the result's flags by boolean formulas over the
  arguments' flags (:299-420), one of them ending in the words "needs more work here"
  (:364).
- **The basic chapters**: eighteen rational types (QQ, QQ* and QQ#, each with five sign
  refinements) listed as subtypes of one another and of the real ones (numbers.tex:36-91),
  with "the Fortress type system tracks these types closely through various arithmetic
  operations" (:93-96); the same for the
  integers (basic-integers.tex:28-66, 70-73), `NN` a synonym for `ZZ_GE` (:63-65), and
  `ZZ_GT` a lattice under divisibility (:531-535). `ZZ extends { QQ, ZZ_star, ... }`
  (:195-196).
- **Against them**: the language chapter's "these types are mutually exclusive"
  (types-vals-vars.tex:500-505; types.tick:977-981), and the instantiation rule
  (types.tick:353-372): `QQ_GT` would be several instantiations of `RationalQuantity`.

### 1. The refresher

The positive rationals, the nonnegative ones, the rationals with infinities, and the
rationals with an indefinite 0/0 are nested subsets. A value's sign is a property of the
value; tracking it in the type lets a checker prove `x / y` is defined, or that a GCD
lattice applies. Every such refinement has the same representation as its parent.

### 2. What each path does today, measured

- The team's `ProjectFortress/tests/conditionalExtension.fss` (Sukyoung Ryu, 2007)
  declares `RationalQuantity` exactly and "can be parsed": walk runs it and prints its line,
  because nothing instantiates the trait (Q3ConditionalExtension.walk.txt). The compiled
  checker rejects it: "Cyclic type hierarchy: Type RationalQuantity transitively extends
  itself" (Q3ConditionalExtension.comp.txt).
- Instantiating the design on walk fails twice over: the trait-level `where { lt OR eq OR gt }`
  is an InterpreterBug (Q3RefineWalk.walk.txt); without it, the conditional extends reports
  "Missing type lt'" (Q3RefineCondWalk.walk.txt). The compiled checker gives the same
  cyclic-hierarchy error for the probe (Q3RefineCondWalk.comp.txt). A parser quirk met on
  the way: `Rat[\false,true\]` in a parameter type is a syntax error and `Rat[\false, true\]`
  parses.
- The same refinements spelled with the later chapter's covariant static parameters
  (each sign flag a type argument, `Never` below `May`; Q3Phantom.fss): the compiled
  checker accepts it and rejects zero passed where a positive is asked (Q3PhantomReject.comp.txt),
  but the generated class does not implement the covariant supertype and the run stops with
  IncompatibleClassChangeError (Q3Phantom.comp.txt); walk has no covariance ("Unification

- Type aliases (`type X = ...`) appear nowhere in Library/ or in the team's tests.

### 3. What the specification says, including the same idea under another spelling

Beyond the designs above: the per-type `check_LT`, `check_GT`, ... methods, which throw
CastError (numbers.tex:228-244): the refinement as a run-time check. Contracts,
`requires { ... }` (functions.tex:418-426): the refinement as a precondition. Coercion from a
generic type (types.tick:393-400) with where-clauses (conversions-coercions.tex:157-160,
196-220): the refinement ordering as coercions, not subtyping. The later Types chapter
comments out the whole Type Aliases section, including the parallel example
`type SimpleFloat[\nat e, nat s\] = DetailedFloat[\Unity,e,s,false,false,false,false,true\]`
(types.tick:1011-1036), and offers covariant parameters instead (types.tick:322-339). The
language chapter's mutual exclusion is the spec's own flat reading.

### 4. Where it sits in the numeric tower

The designs are a second axis on top of the widths: refinement by sign and by
infinity/NaN, same representation. Today's library has only the width axis, and nests it.
Route A flattens the width axis; the refinement axis, if kept as subtyping, is a lattice of
eighteen types per base type that the instantiation rule forbids in its
`RationalQuantity` spelling.

### 5. What the library already does in the same family

It has: `QQ` as one trait over `Ratio` and the integers (fsi:373-407; fss:524-610);
